hero.heading: Expert Blown-In Insulation Services Across the USA
hero.introduction:
Looking for a proven way to make your home more efficient without a major renovation? Blown-in (loose-fill) insulation installs quickly: our crew uses a hose system to blanket your attic floor or fill wall cavities with a thick, uniform layer of insulation.
It is ideal for topping off settled insulation, finishing new spaces, and taming drafty older homes, and Koala Insulation can help with all three.

trusted.title: Blown-In Insulation Pros Across the USA
trusted.content: Hot, humid summers in one region and long, frigid winters in another can make homes uncomfortable and force HVAC systems to work overtime. Even so, many attics in the country are underinsulated, with only a few inches of coverage where modern guidelines call for far more. Best uses for blown-in insulation: Attic floors, where a fresh layer quickly raises your R-value to today’s standards. Knee walls & sloped ceilings where batts are tough to fit. Wall cavities in certain retrofit projects, following industry best practices.

superior.title: Thermal Home Upgrade
superior.content: Blown-in insulation offers homeowners and businesses across the country a powerful way to upgrade comfort and efficiency. Loose-fill products create a continuous thermal blanket over your attic floor or inside cavities, working like traditional insulation while delivering fast, even coverage over new or existing material.
items: Blocks Conductive Heat Loss: By thickening the barrier between living space and attic, blown-in insulation slows the heat that would otherwise pass through the ceilings and walls of your home as outdoor conditions swing.

Cuts Air Leakage: Paired with our targeted air sealing, a blown-in blanket helps close off the small pathways around framing, wiring, and plumbing where conditioned air leaks out of your home and outdoor air sneaks in.
Limits Condensation: Better attic R-value plus preserved ventilation means fewer cold surfaces where moisture can condense, protecting both your home and the insulation itself.

cards.pest_and_wildlife_protection: Worried about unwanted attic guests? Cellulose is the one blown-in material treated with pest-deterrent additives, and pairing it with thorough air sealing helps keep insects and critters out of attics across the country.
cards.soundproofing: Noise reduction is a welcome bonus for homeowners across the country: the dense loose-fill layer soaks up outside sounds and dampens noise moving between levels, from street traffic to kids playing overhead.
cards.environmentally_friendly: Efficiency and sustainability go hand in hand here. Blown-in insulation is produced from recycled materials, and because studies show insulation can reduce heating and cooling energy use by as much as 40%, every winter and summer across the country costs the planet (and you) a little less.

faqs.title: How Much Does Attic Blown-In Insulation Cost in the USA?
faqs.content:
Blown-in insulation is one of the more affordable ways to upgrade home comfort, and the final investment comes down to a handful of factors.
Square footage sets the baseline, the type of insulation (such as cellulose or fiberglass) shapes material costs, and the effort required to install it, things like attic access, prep, and air sealing, rounds out the scope.
Whatever the scope, the upgrade works in your favor over time: better attic coverage means less heat loss and lower heating and cooling bills.

Many state and local governments and local utilities also offer rebates or incentives that can offset a portion of the project. Every home across the country is unique. For an accurate estimate tailored to your property and goals, contact the team today to schedule a free assessment.

faqs.title: Blown-In Insulation vs. Rolls: Which Is Better?
faqs.content: In most attics across the country, yes. The advantage is coverage: blown-in material forms a seamless, continuous layer that conforms around framing, wiring, and plumbing, where rolls (batts) leave seams and voids. Small gaps sound trivial, but they translate into drafts, hot and cold rooms, and lower real-world R-value.
faqs.imageAlt: Illustration comparing continuous blown-in coverage with gaps between rolled batts.

faqs.title: How Much Blown-In Insulation Does My Attic Need?
faqs.content:
The right amount comes down to three inputs: the square footage of the space, the insulation depth required, and where you live (see the map below). Climate drives the recommended attic R-value, with colder regions needing thicker insulation to slow heat loss and warmer regions needing enough depth to block heat gain. Attic size and target R-value together set how much material consistent coverage requires. Across the U.S., recommended attic levels range from roughly R-30 in the warmest climate zones to R-60 in the coldest.

Rather than estimating, professional installers work from climate-zone guidelines, your existing insulation depth, and manufacturer coverage charts. That approach matches depth to the recommended R-value for the region, builds in allowance for settling, and prevents the coverage gaps that undercut performance. Check the diagram below to see how recommended attic levels change across regions, and why the right depth here is not the same as somewhere else.

trusted.title: Is It Time to Remove Your Insulation?
trusted.content: No matter your climate, attic insulation eventually stops performing, and removal is worth considering once you notice: Uneven temperatures and rising energy bills as settled or thin insulation lets conditioned air escape Moisture, mold, or a musty odor from humidity, condensation, or roof leaks in the attic Rodent or pest contamination, with droppings and nesting that break down the material Storm or weather damage ranging from southern hurricane moisture to northern ice dams depending on your region Renovations or wiring upgrades that require the attic to be cleared first Allergy symptoms or poor air quality tied to aging, deteriorating insulation

faqs.title: Is it better to remove old insulation or add more over what is there?
faqs.content: If your attic insulation is dry, clean, and undamaged, adding more over it can be a cost-effective way to reach the R-value recommended for your climate zone. Removal is the better choice when the material is matted, moldy, pest-contaminated, or moisture-damaged, since covering a compromised layer traps the problem. Your local team can assess the attic and recommend the right path for your home.

An in-person look is the only way to give you an accurate number for your home.

additionalFaqs.title: What are the best applications for spray foam insulation?
additionalFaqs.content:
Spray foam insulation is a premium, versatile option for a few specific applications. After your initial assessment, we may recommend spray foam for:
  • Attics: Open-cell spray foam on attic floors seals air leaks and prevents treated air in the living space from escaping into the attic.
  • Basements: Closed-cell spray foam acts as a vapor barrier in moisture-prone basements, crawl spaces, and cellars.
  • Exterior Walls: While not always necessarily the most cost-effective option, spray foam fills irregular gaps in wall cavities while providing an effective moisture barrier.
  • Floors: Spray foam is sometimes sprayed between floor joists in suspended timber floors (non-slab).
  • Roofs: Closed-cell spray foam installed under the roof deck prevents air leaks and protects against moisture issues.

additionalFaqs.title: Do My Rim Joists Need An Airtight Seal?
additionalFaqs.content: Rim joists absolutely benefit from an airtight seal. Sealing this area with spray foam insulation prevents drafts, moisture intrusion, and heat loss where the foundation meets the framing, one of the most common sources of energy waste in a home. By creating a continuous air barrier, you’ll enjoy warmer floors, lower utility bills, and better indoor air quality year-round.
